title: Eight of 12 AI scribes may be medical devices, TGA finds
key_facts: Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) reviewed 12 digital scribe products
Eight have functions likely to meet the legal definition of a medical device; none of the suppliers had identified theirs as one
Of the other four, two need more information and two seem unlikely to qualify
Reviewed products include Heidi Health, Lyrebird Health and Microsoft Dragon Medical One; TGA has not named the eight
TGA found about 100 scribe suppliers; 40 answered a voluntary survey
Some products produce clinical conclusions or recommendations that could affect care; disclaimers are not enough to avoid regulation
The review did not test safety, performance, privacy or compliance, so it does not show products are unsafe or that the law was broken
quote_evidence: Eight of 12 digital scribe products examined by the Therapeutic Goods Administration have functions likely to meet the legal definition of a medical device.
"Statements or disclaimers are not sufficient in determining if a product is, or is not, a medical device," the report said.
The finding that eight products were likely to have medical device functions therefore does not establish that those products are unsafe or that individual suppliers have breached the law.
why_it_matters_hint: AI scribes that start giving clinical advice may need to be registered as medical devices.
notes: Heidi Health gave a statement; iMedX said TGA raised no concerns about its InstaNote.
